title: Timing is kindness (Avot 4:18)
hookLine: the right words at the wrong moment: don't calm a friend at the height of anger, or comfort while their dead lies before them
tomorrow: the group chat is laughing at her. do you laugh too?

lines: CAN THEY COME AT THE WRONG TIME?
cards: Your friend is crying right now, in the hallway, after the worst day of her year. And you have the perfect thing to say. It's true, it's kind, it's ready.
Is right now the time to say it? Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar gives four moments when the answer is no. One question for today: can the right words come at the wrong time?

teach.b: Here are his four, in plain words. Don't try to calm your friend at the height of their anger. Don't comfort them while their dead still lies before them.
Don't question them in the hour they make a vow. And don't try to see them in the hour of their shame. Every one of those is a good act.

teach.h: GOOD ACTS AT THE WRONG MOMENT.
teach.b: And every one, at the wrong moment, lands as a blow. So yes: the right words can come at the wrong time. The kindness is in the waiting.
Here's a neighbor who'd recognize this. In a Buddhist sutta, a prince tries to trap the Buddha with a question: would you ever say something unwelcome?
The Buddha answers that he speaks only what's true and helpful, and that he knows the right time to say it, even when it isn't welcome. Both teachers say a true word isn't enough. Its moment matters.

teach.h: HOLD BACK, OR WAIT FOR ITS TIME.
teach.b: And an honest difference: Rabbi Shimon names four human moments, anger, grief, a vow, shame, and says hold back.
The Buddha's answer is about his own speech on the path to the end of suffering, and for him a hard truth may still need saying, at its time. One waits for the friend. The other waits for the moment.

how: In Jewish mourning, visitors to a shiva house traditionally wait for the mourner to speak first, and comfort is offered after the burial rather than before it.

o: kindness means being on time to every appointment
always answer a friend's message as fast as you can
a good word, said at the right moment, is part of being kind

games.q: four moments to hold back — tap the pairs.
p: while their dead lies before them
in the hour of their shame
true, helpful, and at the right time

s: if what you say is true and kind, any moment is the right one
Rabbi Shimon's four moments are all good acts that land badly at the wrong time.
Avot and the Buddha's answer say exactly the same thing
both care about timing; Avot says hold back in four moments, the Buddha says a hard truth may still need saying, at its time.
Rabbi Shimon's list includes not trying to see someone in their shame
anger, grief, a vow, shame: four moments to hold back.

games.q: your roommate just found out she failed the bar exam, and she's slamming cupboards. you know a great study plan for next time. what fits Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar?
o: make her tea, stay close, and save the plan until she's ready to hear it.
share the plan right away, since it's true and it'll help her feel better.
tell her to calm down first, so she can think about next time clearly.
games.why: don't try to calm your friend at the height of anger. the plan is a good act; its time is later.

practice: Listen for one sound that's happening now: a fan, traffic, a bird, the hum of a fridge. Follow it all the way through, and if it stops, notice the exact moment it ends.
Let the sit be practice in waiting for a thing to finish before you answer it.

wordCard.voice: Timing is kindness. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: don't calm a friend at the height of anger, or comfort them while their dead lies before them.

orig.note: Hebrew: in the hour of his anger, the first of Rabbi Shimon's four moments.

carryVoice: Keep this one: timing is kindness, and sometimes the kind word is later. Forty-two of sixty, in its time.

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:18 (Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: do not appease your fellow in the hour of his anger…)
Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the Buddha knows the right time to say what is true and beneficial, even if unwelcome)
